Stated Claim / Post Context:
‘Our system was overwhelmed’: Huge Mississippi turnout spurs calls for expanded access

After historic turnout during the midterms, Mississippi has a chance to reform its archaic, suppressive election system, civil rights and grassroots pro-voting organizations say.

Actual Article Body:
By Jacob Knutson

November 9, 2026

to see more of our voting rights news coverage when you search.

JACKSON, MISS. — Mississippi has some of the most restrictive voting laws in the country, relics of its infamous legacy of shutting Black people out of power.

But now, after historic turnout during the midterms, the state has a chance to reform its archaic, suppressive election system, civil rights and grassroots pro-voting organizations say.

“I think now there is a possibility for a better conversation, because it benefits everybody, not just a blue, red or gray voter,” Arekia Bennett-Scott, executive director of Mississippi Votes (MSVotes), told Democracy Docket.

Those reforms could include no-excuse mail voting, early voting and same-day and online registration — practices common in many other states with pro-voting policies.

“We don’t have any of that,” said Bennett-Scott, whose organization has helped over 100,000 people register to vote or update their registration since its inception in 2016. “Do you know how many college students I could help register to vote — regardless of whether they were white or Black or Republican or Democrat or independent?”

Join 350,000 readers who rely on our daily and weekly newsletters for the latest in voting, elections and democracy.

The calls for reform come as Democrat Scott Colom appears poised to unseat incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) and become the state’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era.* Last week, in an interview with Democracy Docket, he also called for reforms to “empower the voters to pick their leaders and not the leaders to pick the voters that matter.”

Colom has suggested several national changes, including making Election Day a national holiday and ending the practice of drawing electoral districts to benefit political parties.

Among the reasons for the new interest in pro-voting policies: The massive midterm turnout has shown what the people of Mississippi are capable of — and the limitations of the state’s election system.

Speaking Sunday evening at the M.W. Stringer Masonic Grand Lodge — a civil rights landmark in the state — NAACP President Derrick Johnson said the surge in voter participation laid bare the state election system’s defects.

“Our system was overwhelmed because voters turned out,” Johnson said.

But he added that the past week also emphasized a simple solution: reform.
